**Each credential reaches only what it was given.** A photo app can write images, read the rest, and see no messages.

## Credentials

Two kinds of credential call the API, each sent as `Authorization: Bearer <credential>`:

| Credential | Looks like | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A key | `marfa_k1_…` | What it was made with |
| An app's access token | `marfa_at_…` | What the owner approved for the app |

An agent connecting over MCP uses the same two, and **MCP does what the API lets the same credential do.** The server's own machine has one more authority, the [private socket](/run/run-on-a-server#the-private-socket).

### What the owner's browser reaches

The owner's browser session **counts only on the sign-in and approval pages:** claiming the instance, signing in and out, the screens that approve an app or a device, and the page for the password and passkeys. It never reads an item or changes a setting, so a browser left signed in, a copied cookie or a page that rides on it reaches no data.

## What a credential reaches

A credential's **maps** say which data it reads and writes, and its **permissions** which other operations it may use. The photo app's key:

<Terminal>

```bash
marfa keys create --label "Photo app" --source photo-app \
  --type-permission core.file.image=write \
  --type-permission 'core.*=read' \
  --type-permission core.message=none \
  --edge-permission about=write
```

```text
marfa_k1_…
key 01a1f1a2-a184-736a-b69c-1e18d5770812 (Photo app); the plaintext is shown once, keep it now
  core.file.image  Read and edit
  Built-in types   Read only
  core.message     No access
  edge.about       Read and edit
```

</Terminal>

A map names things at a level, `read` or `write`, and `write` includes reading. Anything a map doesn't name is out of reach. A credential has five maps: **types** of item, **edge** types, **extension** namespaces, **metadata** (registering types and edge types) and the owner's **profile**. Only the type map takes a third level, `none`, which shuts out a type its wildcard covers.

**A permission opens a group of operations, such as making keys, and no items:** a key with no type map reads no item, whatever permissions it holds. The one exception is `blobs.manage`, which reads file bytes ([Files](/build/files#who-may-read-a-blob)). The Catalog's [Permissions](/catalog/permissions) page lists the maps, the fifteen permissions and the rules for each.

## What a refusal reveals

An item of a type the credential **can't read** answers `404 item_not_found`, as an item that doesn't exist does, so a refusal reveals nothing. So do its edges, and a blob only such items name. An item the credential can read but not write is refused `403 type_not_permitted`. The photo app's key reads a message as missing, reads a note, and is refused when it changes the note.

<KeyReach />

## How a credential gets its access

**An app signs in with OAuth.** The instance is its own authorization server, and every app is a public client that holds no secret. The app names the **scopes** it wants, the access it asks for, and the owner approves **Full access** or **Choose access** to give it less. An app that names none is registered for **content**, the items of every type outside `system`, `marfa` and `app`, and for their edges. The app then holds a **grant**, exactly what the owner approved, and each item it writes carries the **source** `oauth:` followed by the app's client ID. The owner can narrow it, which revokes each key the app made that holds more. A grant lasts until the owner disconnects the app or it goes unused for `grant_inactivity_days`, a year by default. [Connect an app with OAuth](/build/connect-an-app) shows the app's side, and [Manage apps](/use/see-and-revoke-access#give-less-access-instead) the owner's.

**A key suits a script, your own agent or a [connector](/build/connectors).** The owner makes one from the CLI, and any key or app holding `keys.mint` can make another. A made key holds only what its maker holds, and expires no later. A key an app makes stays within the app's grant and can name no extension namespace. [Manage keys](/use/manage-keys) shows how.

## An app's own types

**An `app.<vendor>` namespace belongs to the OAuth client that registered its first type,** which needs `metadata.types:write`. That client reaches its items without naming them. **Any other client needs a grant that names `app.<vendor>.*` or `app.*`,** never content or all data, and that includes the same app registered again on another computer. Marfa drops such a scope while no type sits under the vendor. A key an app makes reaches them only as its type map names them. The owner holds a vendor they started, and registering under another client's vendor is refused `403 forbidden`. The owner can [give a vendor to another app](/use/see-and-revoke-access#give-an-apps-types-to-another-app).

The rules behind this page are in the [keys and sign-in](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/keys-and-oauth.md) and [authentication](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/authentication.md#where-a-browser-session-counts) chapters of the contract.
